image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Bubble scatter plot** (scatter plot with varying point sizes and text labels for selected categories).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **No faceting or small multiples**
- **No stacking**
- Single-panel scatter plot with:
  - points positioned by two quantitative axes
  - **bubble size** encoding an additional quantitative variable
  - **text labels** for selected points/categories

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Level of contact | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Activity indoors | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Venue / activity category (e.g., Museums, Gyms, Malls, Parks, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Text label attached to points |
| Magnitude represented by bubble size (unnamed in image) | Quantitative | Bubble area/size |
| Point color (light vs darker green groups) | Categorical/nominal or grouping variable (unnamed in image) | Color/hue and outline color |

comments.raw_comment: After reading the reveal article, I realized that the graph is stating which places people think are the safest to go, though I thought it was stating which places people went to most during the pandemic. Gyms and nail salons require more contact with others, compared to malls and restaurants. Governors are taking into mind the risk of spreading the virus to decide which places are the safest to open up first. Based on the graph, the safest places to open first would be outdoor places with greater contact because if you’re outside, such as at the park or the beach, there’s less interacting with people and touching other surfaces, and you’re able to spread out more, depending on the amount of people. In fact, outdoor areas have already opened in most places. With ranking fast food restaurants, gyms, and sit-down restaurants on which should open first, I think fast food should open first. They are open now, but only offer takeout or mobile orders, which is a smart take. Secondly, should be sit-down restaurants because you are required to eat at the restaurant and sit at tables where others have sat, you have to interact with workers when ordering, and they reuse cutlery. Gyms should open last because you're required to share the equipment, and social distancing can be difficult as well as cleaning the facility and machines each time. I believe it's best to wait to open smaller businesses and crowded places like amusement parks, and wait until the virus starts to clear up more.

comments.raw_comment:
When first looking at this graph, I would assume that this chart is reflecting the virus and the amount of contact. When looking at the graph, it is pretty obvious that indoor activities normally involve high levels of contact between people and surfaces.  I also noticed that the much bigger masses or "bubbles" consist of much more contact, as they are all activities that occur indoors. This directly can affect the spread of the virus, even with fast food where as some people would consider drive thru fast food is non-contact, the food is touched by many many workers and has passed by so many surfaces. This is where we have to be careful with what shops we choose to stay open, and what circumstances they must operate under. 

After reading the reveal and other students' replies, I realized that this graph was actually used in an article earlier this month in which NYT asked people where they thought the safest places were to go and interact. Now that I know this information, I think that public stores and small businesses and places with the least amount of contact should be opened first. I also think that the amount of time people spend in different stores and places should also be a vital factor when deciding  how soon they open to the public. It’s also crucial that we don't open many stores at once, it's very important to start gradually and responsibly.

comments.raw_comment:
I think it would not be irrelevant to present the observation that, as shown in this graph, the level of contact in an establishment depends not on weekly visits, total number of venues, aggrupation of people, or rate of indoors activity, yet rather the conduct and manner expected of the visitants in any given location. 
Said claim, of perhaps obvious quality, is evidenced quite visually by places such as nail salons, beauty salons, gyms, sports clubs, and casinos overtaking locales of the likes of malls, restaurants, and gas stations in the “level of contact” scale, despite their lower number and weekly visits.    

Such a conclusion may be what points us to the order in which we must reopen certain businesses, besides the mien we might consider promoting as an alternative to absolute restrictions.

Additionally, a headline for the graph observed above might be: The Easing of Confining Tensions in Light of a Pandemic.

comments.raw_comment: Human beings are constantly seeking shelter, from the rain the heat, or the cold. Right now we are seeking shelter from other people, trying to protect ourselves from being the part of the positive. Even though most people are following the law and staying home, others are fighting for food, to pay the bills or to not be kicked out of their homes. As this happens many people want the economy to reopen, but how will we do this if we can't live like we used to. Coffee shops and sit down restaurants are a danger we can't faced, or even going to the gym to do your physical activity can lead you to the hospital. These are indoors place but even going to the park can be dangerous if you don't stay away from others. comments.raw_comment: In this graph, I see that the larger bubbles consist of things such as restaurants, fast food, malls, etc. One thing these all have in common - they are indoors. While you may debate that fast food isn't an "indoor" thing, since you usually get the food through your car, that bag of food passes through that entire building before you get it. I feel like during this pandemic, the things that should be eased into openings are the outdoor activities, since in those cases you are less likely to contract the virus. comments.raw_comment:
“Ranking Suddenly Dangerous Buildings.”

Just looking at the graph, I can already see a ton of overlap in medium contact indoor activities. Strangely though, even though sit-down restaurants and malls closed down relatively early, the North Carolina state government left the fast food restaurants open. I’m glad they did though, it’s hard finding food places when all the restaurants are closed. I also remember that gyms, amusement parks, and nail salons were all closed very early on in the pandemic. Though they all lie on different places on the indoors to outdoors scale, I can see that they’re all past level 6 of contact. This is very different from parks and museums which didn’t close as early on. It wasn’t until bored people started flocking to the parks that they closed down. I don’t think that should have happened because parks are so low on the contact scale and are also situated outside. This means that any virus germs that a person could have wouldn’t be passed along as easily as germs in an indoor location would. The same thing happened with the beaches even though they’re not on this graph. 

In order for the state government to start opening things safely, I suggest going from the bottom left corner and ending in the top right corner. Opening buildings that contain activities that are outdoors and alone to those that are indoors and interconnected is the best course of action. Although I do hope that restaurants start opening up again soon. Fingers crossed.

comments.raw_comment: While looking at this graph the first thing that you notice is the eye catching cluster of green circles at the top of the graph, which feature the places that have become a red light during this pandemic. Although I found that I was shocked at how low amusement parks were. They had about the same level of contact as malls and sit-down restaurants (about 6), but salons, gyms, and clubs had way more. This made me curious because I would've thought that amusement parks would be higher in the level of contact because almost every amusement park can be found bustling with people and your always waiting in long , crowded lines for rides. It also hit me that because parks are at a constant 'go,go,go' they don't really get to keep rides clean throughout the day. Where as salons and clubs clean some surfaces throughout the day. At parks your in close proximity with strangers and touching objects that hundreds of people have touched. Something else that shocked me about the salons was that, in Hawai'i, I heard on the news that salons and other places could be opening soon, but if there is such a high rate of contact that people have, that's even higher than restaurants, malls, and stores, I would think about that they wouldn't open it up.  I also find that in a time where our economy is so uncertain people wouldn't spend money on nails and hair. With that I think a good title for this graph is "Do We Know Where True Contact Lies?"

The first thing that I noticed when I viewed this graph was that smaller, indoor spaces where the ones that had the most social interactions occurring within. Which makes sense considering that these places are closed in and full of people shopping or eating. I also noticed that Amusement parks weren't considered to be places with a lot of social interaction which, while they are outdoors mostly and generally spacious, I found weird considering just how many people you see when you go to a place like Disney World in the summer (which is a lot). 

I did wonder when this data was recorded, considering that might affect the information obtained. At the beginning of this year, there might have been a lot of people going to Amusement parks or Museums, therefore increasing the chances of social interaction. Lately, however, people have been rarely leaving their homes other than for necessities. 

All in all, it's the places that have the potential for the most social interactions that will be closed the longest. And while it might have to do with the fact that they're indoor business or other circumstances, I hope that they are taking the necessary precautions so as to not put people at risk.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Each state has been determining when they should start reopening up for businesses and public places.  Which places have the lowest contagion risk?  What order should they be reopened? 

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

This is our final graph for the school year. Please visit our archive at www.nytimes.com/column/whats-going-on-in-this-graph to find dozens of other graphs you can use between now and September, when we will resume this feature. You can also sign up for our free weekly newsletter at www.nytimes.com/newsletters/signup/LN for our free weekly newsletter to make sure you don’t miss any of our new graphs.  

Search for our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom?” for indices by context and by type of graph.  The link for the Stat Nuggets archives is tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Keep noticing and wondering.  Stay tuned.

comments.raw_comment:
Hi! 
I wonder...
I wonder who the specific subjects of this vote were and if it was a varied enough group of people or enough people to really make this data relevant. I also wonder why the specific industries that were looked at were taken into considerations over others that are arguably more pressing and more needed to be reopened. I also wonder why someone would consider an amusement park so low on the contact scale when there is often very little cleaning and masses of people coming in in places like that. That rating alone leads me to question the validity of the entire graph as a real statistic on the interaction and enclosure of these. Lastly, I wonder if when given the scale of 1-10 to vote on if there were any guides like if at going to a tick mark three place you would feel the need to wash your hands or anything like that so in short what the scale is.

I predict...
I predict that as times wear on people will begin to feel differently, and I think in a year when we have been living more cautiously for a while people will begin to see that many of the things put as highly interactive can be done in safer, less contaminating ways. In just two months there has been a lot of innovation in how to run things while social distancing and I think people overestimate the amount of contact and danger of certain things when they can fairly easily be done with minimal contact.


Catchy Headline: The Public's Take On What Is The Most Dangerous Activity Right Now
